title: What you can learn from how Spotify keeps customers from cancelling
hook: Spotify runs a simple system on three things about every customer. The idea is over fifty years old, and almost no business near 100k uses it.
caption:
What you can learn from Spotify. How they stop you from leaving, and what other businesses can copy from them.

Spotify runs a simple system on three signals about every user. How recently they listened, how often they come back, and how much they spend or cost the business to serve.

That is the whole engine.

The idea is over fifty years old, and I have seen very few businesses near 100k use it, even though it costs nothing to set up and explains most of what retention does and does not move.

Here is why it matters.

Your customers are not all worth the same amount to you. Some buy every week, and some buy twice a year. Two customers can look active on a chart and pull your business in opposite directions, and you do not know which is which until you rank them by those three signals.

Here is how to use it in your business.

1. Pull the list of customers from the last ninety days.
2. For each one, note three things. How recently they bought, how often they buy, and how much they spend. A rough estimate is fine for now.
3. Look at the top ten percent of the list. That slice is where most of the money sits.

Treat that top slice like a real person, and not like a line item. Write them a different email, offer them a different plan, and notice when they stop buying on the day it happens, not the month after.

Spotify spends a fortune on data science. They did not invent this system. They used what was already there.

title: The retention problem every business faces near 100k
hook: At 100k, the revenue line looks fine. The real question is who stays, not how many leave.
caption:
# The retention problem for businesses near 100k

## What the chart does not tell you

At 100k, the revenue line looks fine. Each month is a little bigger than the last. Refunds stay below ten percent. Churn hovers in the single digits. If you close the laptop and look around the room, nothing feels like it is on fire.

Compound a small monthly loss over eighteen months, and you have quietly replaced more than half of your customer base. The top-line growth hides it because new customers are coming in a little faster than old ones are leaving. The day that gap narrows, which it always does, the picture changes in an afternoon.

## The real question is who stays, and not how many leave

Two customers sign up the same week. One pays once and disappears. One pays, comes back, buys again, and brings a teammate along. Same product, same price, but a different kind of buyer entirely.

The business at 100k that stalls is the one filling up with the first kind of buyer. The business at 100k that breaks through is the one slowly tilting the list toward the second kind.

You will not tell them apart on day one. You will tell them apart on day ninety. That is the day the business you actually have becomes visible.

## Why most teams look in the wrong place

When customers leave, most teams rewrite onboarding. They add a product tour. They test subject lines. They hire a growth engineer to fix the funnel.

None of that changes the kind of customer coming through the door. The real leverage is earlier, in the sentence on the landing page, in the promise on the ad, in what the business says it is for.

A vague promise pulls vague customers. A sharp promise pulls sharp customers. The copy is doing the sorting whether you want it to or not.

## What to look at this week

Pull your last ninety days of customers. Count how many are still with you today. Count how many pay more now than when they first started. Count how many brought someone new in.

Those three counts are your real business, more than the monthly revenue chart and more than the total customer count. It is those three counts that tell you the truth.

If the counts are low, the fix is further upstream, not further downstream.

## Three moves that work for any business near 100k

**One. Rewrite the first sentence on your landing page.**

Read it cold. Would a stranger know, in one line, who the business is for and what it solves? If not, rewrite that line before anything else in the funnel. Every other channel feeds off it.

**Two. Pay closer attention to the customers you already have.**

Sort your list by who paid the most, and most recently. The top ten percent of that list is where most of the money lives. A short call, a direct message, an annual plan that saves them real money, and a small add-on that fits their habit. That is where retention gets built, one customer at a time.

**Three. Fill the first two weeks after a sale.**

Most businesses near 100k leave that window empty. One welcome email, and then silence for a month. A customer who just paid is the most open to hearing from you they will ever be. A real sequence in those two weeks carries the next three months.

## What happens if you do nothing

The revenue line keeps climbing for a while. The gap between signups and losses narrows, quarter by quarter. One month the gap closes. The line flattens. The team does not know why.

That is the retention problem for businesses near 100k. It is slow and then it is fast, and it is almost always diagnosed after it has already cost a year of runway.

## What to do if you are here now

Pull the three counts this week, and look at them honestly. Rewrite the landing page line. Fill the two-week window. Start with the top ten percent of your customers and work down from there.

title: How Spotify knows you are about to cancel. And how to copy it.
hook: Spotify knows when you are about to cancel a month before you do. They do it with three signals every business already has.
tweets:
Spotify knows when you are about to cancel a month before you do.

They do it with three signals every business already has about its customers. Nothing clever about it, and no new tech involved.

Here is the system, and how to copy it this week.

The three signals are how recently a customer bought, how often they come back, and how much they spend or cost to serve.

That is the whole engine. Over fifty years old as an idea, used by banks, supermarkets, and now Spotify. Almost no business near 100k uses it.

Signal one. How recently they bought.

A customer who bought last week is worth far more than one who bought six months ago, and the gap between those two is usually larger than people think. Sort your list by last purchase and you see the business you actually have.

Signal two. How often they come back.

A customer who buys twice a month is a different animal from one who buys twice a year. The same money lands in the till, but the future looks very different. One customer is a habit, and the other is a memory.

Signal three. How much they spend or cost to serve.

A small slice of customers pays most of the bills. Another small slice pays the least and takes the most support. Treating those two slices the same will always lose you money.

Put it together. Score each customer on the three signals, and rank them into high, middle, and low groups.

You will find most businesses near 100k look the same. Top ten percent funds half of everything. Bottom twenty percent costs almost as much as it brings in.

Here is what to do with the top slice.

Talk to them directly. Send a short survey, offer a direct line, build a plan that locks them in for a year with a real saving. Let them see a face, and not an autoresponder.

Here is what to do with the bottom slice.

Accept that some of those customers are not profitable. Trying to save every last customer costs more than it returns. Freeing up that time for the top slice pays you twice over.

Weekend exercise.

Pull the last ninety days of customers. Score them on the three signals. Look at the top ten percent of the list. Write down one thing they have in common that the rest of the list does not.

Reply with what you find, and I will help you pick the first move.

title: LI Second Post: The one retention audit question worth asking every week
hook: The only question worth asking for every new lead from now on. What would bring this person back on their own, without me chasing them?
caption:
The only question worth asking for every new lead from now on.

If your business is near 100k, start asking this every time a lead comes in.

What would bring this person back on their own, without me chasing them down?

If the answer is a generic email, you are working against the grain of the customer. If the answer is a small win they got on day one, a second problem your product solves for them, or a friend they can share it with, the answer gets more specific the longer you sit with the question.

Sit with the question for a while. The answer shows you what the rest of the funnel is missing.

title: 3 ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio
hook: Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio. You cannot get clients without one, and you cannot build one without clients.
caption:
Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio.

You cannot get clients without a portfolio. You cannot build a portfolio without clients. Every creative strategist trying to make this move has felt that loop.

Here are three roads out of it, ranked from the fastest to the slowest.

One. A public teardown.

Pick one ad running right now. Break it down in a post. Explain what the angle is, why the hook works, and what you would test next. Write one post a week for eight weeks. At the end of two months you have eight public pieces of thinking that the whole market can see. That is a portfolio.

Two. A strategy document.

Pick five businesses you would like to work with. Write a one-page document for each of them. Explain what you see in their ads and what you would do different. Send the document over, unasked. Some of them will ignore you, and some of them will not. You are doing the job to prove that you can do the job.

Three. Spec work.

Pick three brands you care about. Write the creative strategy you wish they had. Publish it with your name on it. This is the slowest of the three roads, but it is the most polished at the end.

Pick one route, and ship it inside two weeks. Most creative strategists stay stuck in the portfolio loop because they spend two months polishing a single thing that never goes out.

title: Portfolio Paradox (FB Page)
hook: Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio. The portfolio does not matter the way people think it does.
caption:
Three ways to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio.

You cannot get clients without a portfolio. You cannot build a portfolio without clients. Every creative strategist trying to make this move has felt that loop.

Here is the thing almost nobody says out loud. The portfolio does not matter the way people think it does.

A prospect who has hired before cannot really evaluate your past work. They do not know what the brief was. They cannot tell if the win was the writer's work, the strategist's work, or the media buyer's work. They do not know which ad out of the twelve in that folder was the one that actually worked.

A prospect who has never hired a creative strategist before has no baseline at all for evaluating samples.

What both kinds of prospects can evaluate is how you think about their business, today, in writing.

That is the one thing inside your control, and you can demonstrate it inside two weeks.

One. A public teardown.

Pick one ad running right now. Break it down in a post. Explain what the angle is, why the hook works, and what you would test next. Write one post a week for eight weeks. At the end of two months you have eight public pieces of thinking the whole market can read. That is a portfolio.

Two. A strategy document.

Pick five businesses you would like to work with. Write a one-page document for each of them. Explain what you see in their ads and what you would do different. Send it, unasked, with no rate and no services page. Just the brief.

Three. Spec work.

Pick three brands, and write the creative strategy you wish they had. Publish the piece with your name on it. This is the slowest of the three routes, and the most polished at the end.

title: 3 things to send instead of a portfolio
hook: Struggling to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio? Here are three things you can send to a prospect instead.
caption:
Struggling to close creative strategy clients without a portfolio?

Here are three things you can send to a prospect instead of a folder of samples. Each one takes about ninety minutes to put together.

1. An ad teardown. Take a screenshot of one of their current ads, and write three sentences on what you would test next and why.
2. A one-page strategy document. Explain who the offer is for, why it is selling right now, and what you would push harder on this quarter.
3. A rewrite of one of their offers with a clear hypothesis attached. Say why you think this version will move the number.

Send one of the three inside a week. The creative strategists who get hired are the ones who send the thinking first.
